title: Reenvisioning sexual health with perspectives from the Global South
byline: Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health
excerpt: Sexual and reproductive health has largely been shaped by perspectives from wealthier developed nations in the Global North. To correct this imbalance, public health experts call for centering Global South knowledge, lived experience and culturally grounded understandings of sexuality—including sexual pleasure.
content_html:
Sexual and reproductive health has largely been shaped by perspectives from wealthier developed nations in the Global North. To correct this imbalance, public health experts call for centering Global South knowledge, lived experience and culturally grounded understandings of sexuality—including sexual pleasure.

Jessie Ford, Ph.D., assistant professor of sociomedical sciences, and co-authors draw on examples from Māori communities and West Africa to show how these perspectives can broaden the way we think about sexual health research, policy and practice.

The commentary article is published in the journal Culture, Health & Sexuality.

"So long as Global North frameworks continue to dictate what counts as sexual freedom, pleasure, or health, programs and interventions may remain partial, exclusionary, and at times harmful," the authors write.

The article observes that a disproportionate share of research originates in the Global North, leaving Global South perspectives marginalized. In many Global South contexts, sexual and reproductive health interventions are focused on disease prevention and family planning, often sidelining considerations of pleasure or holistic health. Agendas shaped in the Global North are often implemented through external financing structures that attach conditions to funding and prioritize externally defined goals.

For example, in Sierra Leone, an influx of international HIV-related funding reshaped national health priorities despite the country's relatively low HIV prevalence, limiting the ability to prioritize other urgent health concerns. More recently, there has been a rise in funding from U.S.-based pro-family conservative groups to political campaigns that support anti-abortion and anti-LGBTQ policies.

The researchers draw on perspectives from the Global South to imagine a new path for sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR). For example, Māori researcher Ngāhuia Murphy draws on Māori cosmologies and the lived experiences of people who menstruate to challenge colonial narratives that frame menstruation as dirty or shameful and justify women's inferiority.

Likewise, Yoruba traditions in West Africa frame knowledge as experiential and somatic as well as rational. In practice, this orientation suggests that SRHR interventions can move beyond risk-focused messaging and survey-based measures to incorporate sensory and embodied approaches—such as guided body awareness or facilitated conversations about touch and feeling.

"The future of sexual health will be defined not by a universalized Global North narrative but by all the voices that insist on liberation as a collective, culturally grounded, and intersectional project. This future will build on existing scientific and quantitative advances while also drawing on lived experience—how things feel, what people remember, and how individuals connect with their communities," they conclude.

Authors include Madison Moore, an MPH student at Columbia Mailman School; Laura Gemmell-Sinnott, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Otago and Fulbright fellow at Columbia Mailman; and Ford.

More information

Madison Moore et al, Decolonising sexual pleasure: elevating Global South narratives in sexual health, Culture, Health & Sexuality (2026). DOI: 10.1080/13691058.2026.2688251

content_html_zh:
性健康和生殖健康在很大程度上是由北半球富裕发达国家的观点决定的。 为了纠正这种不平衡，公共卫生专家呼吁集中全球南方国家的知识、生活经验和基于文化的对性（包括性快感）的理解。

社会医学科学助理教授 Jessie Ford 博士和合著者利用毛利社区和西非的例子来展示这些观点如何拓宽我们对性健康研究、政策和实践的思考方式。

评论文章发表在《文化、健康与性》杂志上。

作者写道：“只要北半球框架继续规定性自由、性快感或健康的定义，项目和干预措施就可能仍然是片面的、排他性的，有时甚至是有害的。”

文章指出，不成比例的研究来自北半球，而南半球的观点被边缘化。 在许多南半球国家中，性健康和生殖健康干预措施的重点是疾病预防和计划生育，往往忽视了对快乐或整体健康的考虑。 北半球国家制定的议程通常通过外部融资结构来实施，这些结构对融资附加条件并优先考虑外部确定的目标。

例如，在塞拉利昂，尽管该国的艾滋病毒感染率相对较低，但与艾滋病毒相关的国际资金的涌入重塑了国家卫生优先事项，限制了优先处理其他紧急卫生问题的能力。 最近，美国亲家庭保守团体对支持反堕胎和反 LGBTQ 政策的政治运动的资助有所增加。

研究人员借鉴南半球国家的观点，设想了一条性健康和生殖健康及权利（SRHR）的新道路。 例如，毛利人研究员 Ngāhuia Murphy 利用毛利人的宇宙论和经期者的生活经历来挑战殖民主义叙事，这些叙事将月经视为肮脏或可耻的，并证明女性的自卑是合理的。

同样，西非的约鲁巴传统将知识视为经验性、躯体性和理性性的。 在实践中，这种方向表明 SRHR 干预措施可以超越以风险为中心的信息传递和基于调查的措施，纳入感官和具体方法，例如引导身体意识或促进有关触摸和感觉的对话。

“性健康的未来将不是由全球北方的普遍叙述来定义，而是由所有坚持将解放作为一个集体的、基于文化的、跨领域的项目的声音来定义。 这个未来将建立在现有的科学和定量进步的基础上，同时也借鉴生活经验——事物的感觉、人们的记忆以及个人如何与社区联系，”他们总结道。

作者包括哥伦比亚邮差学院公共卫生硕士学生麦迪逊·摩尔 (Madison Moore)；劳拉·格梅尔-辛诺特，博士 奥塔哥大学候选人和哥伦比亚邮报公司富布赖特研究员；和福特。
